transcript.speaker: clinician1
transcript.text: Thanks for coming in. I'll ask about attention, first now as an adult, then as a child. Do you often have trouble keeping your attention on tasks at work?

transcript.speaker: alex1
transcript.text: Yeah, in meetings especially. If it goes past twenty minutes I'm gone, I'm thinking about something else.

transcript.speaker: clinician1
transcript.text: How often does that happen?

transcript.speaker: alex1
transcript.text: Most meetings. So three or four times a week.

transcript.speaker: clinician1
transcript.text: Do you make careless mistakes in your work, like in emails or reports?

transcript.speaker: alex1
transcript.text: Not really. My manager actually says my reports are pretty clean. I double-check everything.

transcript.speaker: clinician1
transcript.text: Do you often lose things you need, like keys, phone, wallet?

transcript.speaker: alex1
transcript.text: My phone, constantly. Probably every day I'm hunting for it.

transcript.speaker: clinician1
transcript.text: And keys?

transcript.speaker: alex1
transcript.text: Keys, no. I have a hook by the door. That one I solved.

transcript.speaker: clinician1
transcript.text: Do you have trouble finishing tasks, like household projects?

transcript.speaker: alex1
transcript.text: Sometimes. I've got a half-painted bathroom right now. Actually, it's been like that a month mostly because we ran out of paint.

transcript.speaker: clinician1
transcript.text: Are you easily distracted by things going on around you?

transcript.speaker: alex1
transcript.text: Hm.

transcript.speaker: clinician1
transcript.text: Let's go back to childhood, ages five to twelve. Did teachers comment on your attention?

transcript.speaker: alex1
transcript.text: Oh, constantly. Every report card said "daydreams" or "doesn't finish work."

transcript.speaker: clinician1
transcript.text: Did you have trouble with homework?

transcript.speaker: alex1
transcript.text: I'd forget it at home maybe once a week. That stopped by high school.

transcript.speaker: clinician1
transcript.text: Sam, you've lived with Alex for six years. What do you notice?

transcript.speaker: sam1
transcript.text: He forgets things we've agreed on. I'll ask him to pick up groceries and he comes home without them, maybe twice a month.

transcript.speaker: clinician1
transcript.text: Anything else?

transcript.speaker: sam1
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm the forgetful one with appointments. I rely on his calendar. He's good with appointments.

transcript.speaker: clinician1
transcript.text: Alex, do you agree about the groceries?

transcript.speaker: alex1
transcript.text: I think it's less than that. Maybe once a month, if that.

transcript.speaker: clinician1
transcript.text: Is any of this causing problems at work?

transcript.speaker: alex1
transcript.text: I got a comment in my review about seeming checked out in meetings. That's it. I wasn't written up or anything.

sentences.S1: Alex reports losing attention in most meetings, about three to four times a week.
sentences.S2: He reports misplacing his phone daily but has a system for keys.
sentences.S3: He describes some difficulty finishing household projects, although the current unfinished project is partly because they ran out of paint.
sentences.S4: His partner reports he forgets agreed errands about twice a month; Alex estimates once a month.
sentences.S5: Childhood report cards repeatedly noted daydreaming and unfinished work.
sentences.S6: He received a review comment about seeming disengaged in meetings.
sentences.S7: He denies careless mistakes at work.
